plan.topic: Does Ozempic curb alcohol cravings? What the semaglutide trials in alcohol use disorder actually show
plan.angle: Title: 'Does Semaglutide (Ozempic) Curb Alcohol Cravings? What 3 Trials in Alcohol Use Disorder Show'. Slide order: question → mechanism → Lancet 2026 RCT (AUD + obesity, 26 weeks) → JAMA Psychiatry 2025 (9 weeks, small, low dose) → AJP 2026 oral trial (8 weeks, n=50) → mouse data labelled 'in mice' → what we don't know (not approved for AUD, short trials, mostly small, people with obesity in the largest trial) → where to get help (SAMHSA, GP/NHS, Drinkline, plus a warning that heavy drinkers shouldn't stop abruptly without medical advice) → questions for your clinician. Source tag on every slide, no doses, exact prescriber line.
plan.working_title: Does Ozempic (Semaglutide) Curb Alcohol Cravings? What 2 Small Trials Show
plan.why: A rising brain and reward story with fresh coverage, and Q4 'Dry January' interest is building. The careful 'promising, not approved for this' framing makes it today's myth-busting piece, and it adds a body system no other piece covers. | fact-check: The evidence has moved on, so '2 small trials' is now out of date and would mislead viewers. Verified so far: (a) Hendershot et al., JAMA Psychiatry 2025: low-dose weekly semaglutide vs placebo for 9 weeks in about 48 adults with AUD who weren't seeking treatment. It reduced heavy-drinking days (primary endpoint in the published paper; confirm the endpoint wording) and craving. (b) CU Anschutz oral semaglutide RCT, American Journal of Psychiatry 2026: 50 treatment-seeking adults with moderate to severe AUD, 8 weeks. It reduced heavy-drinking days, drinking intensity, craving and consequences. (c) The Lancet 2026: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT of once-weekly semaglutide in AUD with comorbid obesity, reporting fewer heavy-drinking days at 26 weeks. This is the largest and strongest trial so it must go first, following the 'strongest evidence first' rule. Pull exact n, duration and effect sizes from each paper. Don't use any dosing detail (e.g. 3 mg → 7 mg) on slides; that breaks the no-dosing rule. Keep observational data such as the Healio Aug 2026 item labelled 'linked to'. 'Curb cravings' in the title is fine because craving was a measured outcome, but say 'in adults with alcohol use disorder'. Semaglutide is not approved for AUD anywhere as of Sept 2026. The help slide is good. SAMHSA's helpline 1-800-662-4357 is correct. For the UK, add 'your GP, or Drinkline 0300 123 1110'. Add a note that people should not stop alcohol abruptly without medical advice if they drink heavily, because withdrawal can be dangerous.

package.title: Does Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) Cut Heavy Drinking? What 3 Trials in Alcohol Use Disorder Show

social.instagram_caption:
Does semaglutide (the drug in Ozempic and Wegovy) cut heavy drinking? 🧠 Here's what 3 small trials in alcohol use disorder actually show.

🔹 Largest trial: 108 adults with alcohol use disorder + obesity, 26 weeks, everyone also got talk therapy
🔹 Heavy-drinking days (past 30) fell to ~5 on semaglutide vs ~9 on placebo, down from ~17 at baseline
🔹 Two smaller, shorter trials (48–50 adults, 8–9 weeks): a weekly injection cut lab drinking and craving; a daily pill missed its main goal (lab craving) but cut heavy-drinking days
🔹 Rat studies hint at a brain-reward mechanism; human trials are still testing whether it holds up
🔹 Not approved for alcohol use disorder anywhere, as of Sept 2026

Save this for your next doctor visit 📌

Drink heavily? Don't stop suddenly — withdrawal can be dangerous, so get medical advice first. Seizures, confusion or hallucinations? Call 911/999 or go to ER/A&E now. US: SAMHSA 1-800-662-4357 (free, 24/7). UK: your GP or Drinkline 0300 123 1110.

Have you heard GLP-1s being talked about for drinking? Tell us below 👇

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

social.facebook_caption:
Can semaglutide, the GLP-1 medicine in Ozempic and Wegovy, help with heavy drinking too? Researchers are starting to find out.

The biggest trial so far followed 108 treatment-seeking adults with alcohol use disorder and obesity in Denmark for 26 weeks, with everyone also getting talk therapy. Heavy-drinking days (in the past 30) dropped to about 5 on semaglutide vs about 9 on placebo, down from about 17 at the start. Two smaller, shorter trials (48–50 adults, 8–9 weeks) were early and small: a weekly injection cut lab drinking and craving, while a daily pill missed its main goal (lab-measured craving) but still cut heavy-drinking days. Early rat studies point to a possible brain-reward mechanism, but that's animal research, not proof in people.

Bottom line: promising early signals, not an approved use. Semaglutide isn't approved for alcohol use disorder anywhere as of September 2026. If you drink heavily, don't stop suddenly — withdrawal can be dangerous, so get medical advice first (US: SAMHSA 1-800-662-4357, free 24/7; UK: your GP or Drinkline 0300 123 1110). Seizures, confusion or hallucinations? Call 911/999 or go to ER/A&E now. If drinking is something you're thinking about, your doctor can walk you through real options.

Have you heard about this research before? This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
I checked the carousel against the sources. Nearly all of it holds up.

**What checks out:**
- **Lancet 2026 trial:** 108 treatment-seeking adults with alcohol use disorder (AUD) plus obesity, at one centre in Copenhagen, for 26 weeks, with talking therapy (CBT) for everyone. Heavy-drinking days went from about 17 at the start to about 5 on semaglutide vs about 9 on placebo. The main-goal figures (41.1 vs 26.4 percentage points) match, and the trial had no follow-up afterwards.
- **JAMA Psychiatry 2025 trial:** 48 adults not seeking treatment, 9 weeks, low dose, less drinking in the lab and less craving.
- **Pill trial (Am J Psychiatry 2026):** 50 treatment-seeking adults, 8 weeks. It missed its main goal (craving measured in the lab), and heavy-drinking days were one of its two key secondary goals.
- **Animal study (Aranäs, eBioMedicine 2023):** the mouse/rat split is described correctly (dopamine measured in mice, drinking in rats).
- **Help and safety slides:** the SAMHSA number, NHS Drinkline, the withdrawal warning and the 911/999 red-flag symptoms all match NHS and MedlinePlus. The NIAAA page does list approved AUD medicines.
- **Framing:** hedges (small, short, not approved for AUD, as of Sept 2026), the prescriber line and the animal-vs-human split are all handled well.

**One major problem (slide 4):** the pill trial is described as "no drop in drinks/day". That's wrong. The trial found no *significant difference* vs placebo in drinks per calendar day. But drinks per *drinking* day did fall significantly, according to both the APA press release and AJMC.

**Minor fixes:**
- Slide 3 should add the trial's own estimated difference: 13.7 points. Readers who subtract 41.1 minus 26.4 will get 14.7.
- Slide 4's "BMI 25+" for the pill trial: AJMC confirms everyone had overweight or obesity, but I couldn't find the exact BMI cutoff.
- Slide 7: add Drinkline's opening hours, since it isn't a 24/7 line.

**Sources I couldn't open:** the Lancet, psychiatryonline, eBioMedicine and PubMed pages all blocked me (403 errors). Search results and secondary coverage (Healio, AJMC, GPnotebook) confirm those papers exist with the listed titles and what they say. They are left out of the confirmed source list because the URLs couldn't be fetched. I didn't fetch the JAMA Psychiatry page through to the full figures, but it did return the trial summary.

issues.location: Slide 4 (comparison) – Am J Psychiatry 2026 column 'Found vs placebo' value and body
issues.claim: Missed main goal (lab craving); fewer heavy days, but no drop in drinks/day; less day-to-day craving
issues.problem: This overstates the result. The trial found no significant difference vs placebo in drinks per calendar day, which isn't the same as 'no drop'. Both arms cut back, and drinks per drinking day fell significantly on semaglutide (APA press release; AJMC). The body text has the same problem: 'drinks per day didn't'.
issues.fix: Value: "Missed main goal (lab craving); fewer heavy days; drinks per day (all days) not significantly different; fewer drinks on drinking days; less day-to-day craving". Body sentence: "Of its two key secondary goals, heavy-drinking days improved, but drinks per day (counting all days) didn't differ significantly from placebo."

issues.claim: Main goal: heavy-drinking days fell 41.1 percentage points on semaglutide vs 26.4 on placebo.
issues.problem: The figures are correct, but the trial's own estimated difference (13.7 points, 95% CI 5.4–22.0) isn't given. Readers will subtract and get 14.7. Our craft notes say to name the estimand.
issues.fix: "Main goal: heavy-drinking days fell 41.1 percentage points on semaglutide vs 26.4 on placebo (estimated difference 13.7 points)."

issues.problem: Secondary coverage (AJMC) confirms that everyone in this trial had overweight or obesity, but I couldn't confirm an exact BMI 25 cutoff against the paper.
issues.fix: "Seeking treatment, all with overweight or obesity"

issues.problem: Drinkline isn't 24/7, and putting it right under a '24/7' SAMHSA line suggests it is. NHS lists its hours as weekdays 9am–8pm and weekends 11am–4pm.
